e.etymology: An English and Scottish surname for a weaver, from Old English webba. It has been an occasional American first name since the 19th century.
Used in the US mainly by Spanish-speaking families as a spelling of Saira or Zaira, and sometimes as a form of Sara.
A spelling of Alex, short for Alexander or Alexandra, from Greek alexein, to defend, and aner, man. It can also follow Alix, a medieval French form of Alice.

assoc.t: Alyx Vance of the Half-Life video games

e.etymology: A spelling of Cassidy, from the Irish surname O Caiside, descendant of Caiside, a personal name usually linked to Irish cas, curly-haired.
Sanskrit raja, king, the title of Indian rulers and a common boys' name across South Asia. A separate Arabic name, Raja, means hope and is given to girls and boys.
A modern American name that joins the Ja- prefix to Amira or Mira, or serves as a feminine form of Jamir.
The name of the Hindu god who preserves the universe, one of the three chief deities with Brahma and Shiva. Sanskrit tradition explains it as the one who pervades everything.

assoc.t: Hindu god who preserves the universe

e.etymology: The feminine of Bruno, from Germanic brun, brown. It is a familiar name in Italy and Brazil.
An English and Irish surname taken up as a given name for girls and boys; it is also treated as a spelling of Farran or Faron.
An Irish surname shortened from McQuaid, Gaelic Mac Uaid, son of Uad, a pet form of Walter. Most Americans know it from the acting brothers Dennis and Randy Quaid.
A Greek spelling of Cassia, the name of a cinnamon-like spice tree and also the feminine of the Roman family name Cassius. Saint Kassia was a 9th-century Byzantine abbess and hymn writer.
The Hebrew form of Judah. In Genesis, Leah names her fourth son Yehudah, saying this time she will praise the Lord. His tribe gave its name to the kingdom of Judah and to the Jewish people.
The English name of the long-legged wading bird, also a surname. Heron is in addition the Greek form of the name of Hero of Alexandria, the ancient engineer.
A Spanish-influenced spelling of Heidi, the German pet form of Adelheid, from adal, noble, and heid, kind or sort. Johanna Spyri's 1881 novel Heidi carried the name around the world.
The Russian and Church Slavic form of Reuben, the eldest son of Jacob and Leah in Genesis, whose Hebrew name is explained as behold, a son.
The name of the bright blue-white star at the foot of Orion, from Arabic rijl, foot, in the star's Arabic name, the foot of the great one.

assoc.t: brightest star in the constellation Orion

e.etymology: A Tibetan name meaning merit or good fortune, given to girls and boys in Tibet, Bhutan, Nepal and northern India. A separate Hindi girls' name is written the same way in English.
A 19th-century American form of Zoe, from Greek zoe, life.
Related to Annelies and Anneliese, the Dutch and German blend of Anna and Liese, a short form of Elisabeth. In the US it is also a spelling of Annalee, Anna joined to Lee.
An American spelling of Giovanna, the Italian feminine of Giovanni, John, from Hebrew Yochanan, God is gracious. The first syllable follows the nickname Gia.
A spelling of Ansley, an English surname from place names ending in Old English leah, a woodland clearing. This form brings out the name Ann.
The French spelling of Arabic shaykh, an elder or learned leader. It is a common first name in Senegal, where it honors Sufi teachers such as Cheikh Ahmadou Bamba.
A pet form of names beginning Aur-, such as Aurelia, Aurora and Aura, used on its own in the early 1900s.
A boys' name used mainly in Honduras and by Central American families in the US, close in form to Alvin and Elvin.
Tamil iniya, sweet or pleasant, is used as a girls' name in South India. In the US Iniya is also a spelling in the family of Aniya and Inaya.
A spelling of Kensley, a variant of Kinsley, an English surname from a Yorkshire place name ending in leah, a woodland clearing.
A spelling of Maddox, a Welsh surname meaning son of Madoc, an old name built on mad, fortunate or good. Maddox rose after Angelina Jolie chose it for her son in 2002.
A spelling of Finley, from the Scottish Gaelic name Fionnlagh, built from fionn, fair or white, and laoch, warrior.
Arabic yazid, he increases, from the root for growth and abundance. Yazid I was the second caliph of the Umayyad dynasty.
e.note: Shia Muslims hold the caliph Yazid I responsible for the killing of Husayn at Karbala and avoid the name.

e.etymology: A spelling of Zayden, an American name of the 2000s that sets a Z on the -ayden sound of Jayden, Kayden and Brayden.

A Hebrew name borne by several men in the Old Testament, among them a chief priest of Jerusalem. It joins a root for striving or ruling to Yah, the name of God. American parents now give it mostly to girls.
Arabic zayid, increasing or abundant, from the same root as Zayd and Yazid. Sheikh Zayed bin Sultan Al Nahyan was the founding president of the United Arab Emirates.
